analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal money for the FDA's proposed safety rules for fruit and vegetable growers.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to a House subcommittee, it never advanced before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would have barred any federal money from finalizing, carrying out, or enforcing a proposed FDA rule that sets safety standards for how fruits and vegetables are grown, harvested, packed, and held [S2, S3]. That rule was written to carry out the 2011 food safety law, covering things like water quality, worker hygiene, and handling practices on produce farms. The bill would have stopped those standards from ever taking effect. It was introduced by one representative, attracted no cosponsors, and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Produce growers, packers, and handlers who would have faced the cost of meeting the new safety standards. Meeting water testing, hygiene, and record-keeping requirements takes money and staff, and the burden falls hardest on smaller farms with thinner margins. Blocking the rule would have spared them those costs.

how_it_helps.text: Would have prohibited all federal spending on finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the FDA's proposed produce safety rule, or any successor rule substantially like it [S2, S3].
In practice, that would have spared produce farms the cost of complying with new safety standards for growing, harvesting, packing, and holding fruits and vegetables [S2].
The bill contained a single operative sentence, so its only effect would have been to stop this one rule and anything modeled on it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers of fresh produce. The safety standards the bill would block were designed to reduce contamination in fruits and vegetables, which have been the source of major foodborne illness outbreaks. Without enforceable standards, the risk of getting sick from contaminated produce stays with shoppers, and outbreaks — which are expensive for growers, retailers, and public health systems — remain more likely.

drawbacks.text: Blocking the rule would have left fresh produce — a food most Americans eat raw — without mandatory federal safety standards for water, worker hygiene, and handling, keeping the risk of foodborne illness on consumers [S2, S3].

The good-faith case for the bill was cost: as proposed in January 2013, the standards would have required farms to change water use, worker practices, and record-keeping, and the burden falls disproportionately on smaller growers. An honest supporter would acknowledge the safety trade-off and argue the rule could be tailored rather than blocked outright.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: lower compliance costs for produce farms, felt most by smaller operations. The cost is broad: weaker protection against contaminated produce for everyone who eats it, and no federal backstop if a grower's practices fall short. Deferring or modifying an overly burdensome rule is a defensible policy choice; defunding it entirely with one sentence, with no replacement standard, tips the balance clearly toward the growers and away from the public.

outcome.mechanism: A single representative introduced it, no one cosponsored it, the House Energy and Commerce Committee referred it to its Health subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dan Benishek introduced the bill on May 21, 2013 [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and three days later to that committee's Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No cosponsors signed on in either chamber [S4].
The subcommittee never took it up, no vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Produce growers who would have faced compliance costs are better off, since the proposed standards were never defunded — though the FDA rule proceeded on its own track regardless, and the bill was too narrow to have changed the outcome even if it had moved. Consumers are no worse off than they would have been if the bill had never been introduced.

for.name: Rep. Dan Benishek
for.role: Sponsor, House Agriculture-adjacent member from Michigan's produce region
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter of record.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting the bill die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill and no member of either party cosponsored it, so no party position was ever recorded in a vote.

industries.note: Blocking the rule would have spared these farms the cost of water testing, hygiene, and handling standards. Their savings would come at the price of weaker safety protection for the people who eat their products raw. (The FDA did finalize modified versions of the rule in 2015–2016 that eased several burdens on smaller farms, which weakened the case for outright defunding.)
The bill would have stripped the agency's funding to finalize and enforce the produce rule, leaving it unable to set mandatory standards for fresh produce.
